lesson.title: Measuring Yourself Against Everyone Else
lesson.summary: Social comparison theory holds that people evaluate their own abilities, opinions, and worth largely by comparing themselves to other people, especially when no objective yardstick is available.
lesson.body:
How do you know if you are a good writer, a fast runner, or doing well financially? For many things in life there is no built in ruler, so, as psychologist Leon Festinger proposed in 1954, people rely heavily on comparing themselves with others as a substitute for an objective standard. Festinger argued that this drive to self-evaluate through comparison is a basic and fairly automatic part of how people figure out where they stand, most active precisely in those situations where no clear, non-social measuring stick exists.

Later researchers distinguished two directions this comparison can run. In an upward social comparison, you compare yourself to someone you see as better off or more capable, a classmate who scored higher, a coworker who got promoted faster, an athlete performing at an elite level. Upward comparisons can be motivating, giving you a model to aim for, but they can also sting, highlighting a gap between where you are and where you wish you were. In a downward social comparison, described in later work by psychologist Thomas Wills in the early 1980s, you compare yourself to someone you see as worse off, which tends to be self-protective, making your own situation feel more acceptable by contrast, even if it does nothing to actually improve that situation.

Social comparison connects to attribution in a direct way. Whether a given comparison helps or hurts often depends on how you explain the gap. Attributing a classmate's higher grade to natural talent you simply lack can feel discouraging and threatening, while attributing the same gap to the fact that they studied more, a more controllable, situational explanation, can be motivating rather than deflating. The comparison itself does not determine the emotional impact. The attribution layered on top of it does much of that work.

Social media has arguably supercharged the opportunities for upward comparison, since feeds are largely curated highlight reels rather than representative samples of other people's ordinary days. A number of researchers have found associations between heavy social media use, frequent upward comparison, and lower wellbeing, though it is worth being careful here. This is an area of active research, the direction of cause and effect is genuinely debated, and it is not yet settled how much of the association reflects social media causing worse comparison habits, existing low wellbeing driving heavier use, or some mix of both.
